# Parkinson's disease rehabilitation and adjunct therapies: exercise, physical, speech and occupational therapy, dance, music, acupuncture, cannabis and supplements — concept pack

## Vocabulary

Terms this pack was harvested with, grouped by their relation to the concept; counts are units matched / sources. Zero-hit terms are listed under Coverage. On every unit line, `keywords:` names the terms that matched.

- **self**: Parkinson's disease rehabilitation and adjunct therapies: exercise, physical, speech and occupational therapy, dance, music, acupuncture, cannabis and supplements (119/10)

## Structure and components

- [statement] The Parkinson's Foundation exercise page lists biking, running, Tai Chi, yoga, Pilates, dance, weight training, non-contact boxing and qi gong among exercise types that all have positive effects on PD symptoms; the APTA guideline says results across community-based exercise modes appear comparable for impairment and participation-based measures, suggesting no 1 mode is superior to another, while other comparisons favor 1 intervention over another and the essential components that distinguish more from less effective programs are not clear; a network meta-analysis of mind-body exercises (Bai et al.) concludes that superiority over other exercise modalities remains uncertain. (medium confidence) (verified as of 2026-11-27) — https://www.parkinson.org/living-with-parkinsons/treatment/exercise · keywords: Parkinson's disease rehabilitation and adjunct therapies: exercise, physical, speech and occupational therapy, dance, music, acupuncture, cannabis and supplements · also: https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9046970/, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC13751929/
- [statement] SPARX3 (NCT04284436) is a phase 3 multicenter randomized evaluator-blinded treadmill endurance-exercise trial in persons with PD diagnosed within 3 years and untreated with symptomatic therapy, comparing moderate intensity (60–65% of maximum heart rate) with high intensity (80–85%) at 4 days per week and 30 minutes per session, with change in the MDS-UPDRS motor score (Part III) over 12 months as the primary outcome. (medium confidence) — https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9535216/ · keywords: Parkinson's disease rehabilitation and adjunct therapies: exercise, physical, speech and occupational therapy, dance, music, acupuncture, cannabis and supplements · also: https://clinicaltrials.gov/api/v2/studies/NCT04284436

## How it works

- [statement] Sources describe limited durability of cueing effects: the APTA guideline states that the lasting effects of cueing are unclear because benefits appear to dissipate over time, and that effects appear to dissipate when the cues are removed; the RESCUE crossover trial (153 patients; 3-week home cueing programme using a prototype cueing device) reported that effects of intervention had reduced considerably at 6-week follow-up; and a narrative review of cueing in people with freezing of gait reported that long-term consolidation and transfer of the effects appear to be hampered in that subgroup. (high confidence) — https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9046970/ · keywords: Parkinson's disease rehabilitation and adjunct therapies: exercise, physical, speech and occupational therapy, dance, music, acupuncture, cannabis and supplements · also: https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC2077658/, https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/28890341/

## Measurements and reference values

- [statement] A meta-analysis of therapeutic massage for motor symptoms in PD (Kang et al.; 363 participants in seven RCTs and one randomized pilot-control study) reported greater total effectiveness than control (RR: 1.33, 95% CI 1.14–1.55) and better UPDRS-III scores (SMD = −0.46, 95% CI −0.67, −0.24) but no better daily-living outcomes (SMD = −0.15, 95% CI −0.40, 0.10, p = 0.23), and a separate systematic review of 12 studies (Angelopoulou et al.) concluded that, despite methodological concerns, there is a wide range of safe massage techniques with beneficial effects on both motor and non-motor symptoms of PD. (medium confidence) — https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9483027/ · keywords: Parkinson's disease rehabilitation and adjunct therapies: exercise, physical, speech and occupational therapy, dance, music, acupuncture, cannabis and supplements · also: https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/32147033/
- [statement] Positive findings on cannabis in PD come from open-label or uncontrolled designs that the sources treat with caution: a 2026 single-center open-label prospective cohort of 68 patients initiating medical cannabis reported improvements in the Non-Motor Symptoms Scale total score at 3 months, with a dropout rate of 26.5%, and its authors call the findings exploratory; an earlier systematic review states that positive effects described in uncontrolled studies have not been confirmed by the few and small RCTs; and the Parkinson's Foundation consensus statement says studies suggesting non-motor benefit are generally small, uncontrolled and open label, and that more rigorous research is needed. (high confidence) — https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/42304702/ · keywords: Parkinson's disease rehabilitation and adjunct therapies: exercise, physical, speech and occupational therapy, dance, music, acupuncture, cannabis and supplements · also: https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/32351233/, https://www.parkinson.org/sites/default/files/documents/medical_cannabis_statement_finalv2_5.pdf
- [statement] In the CBD-PD-BRH trial (Parkinsonism & Related Disorders, volume 135, June 2025), sixty PD patients were randomized to sublingual CBD or placebo and 51 were analysed; the authors report that the primary outcome, MoCA delayed recall, showed no group differences, that the CBD group improved naming scores (mean difference 0.37, 95 % CI 0.01 to 0.73) at a mean CBD dose of 26 mg/day, and that alkaline phosphatase was elevated in the CBD group with no serious side effects in either group. (low confidence) — https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/abs/pii/S1353802025005826 · keywords: Parkinson's disease rehabilitation and adjunct therapies: exercise, physical, speech and occupational therapy, dance, music, acupuncture, cannabis and supplements
- [statement] In an exploratory double-blind trial of 21 PD patients without dementia or comorbid psychiatric conditions (placebo, CBD 75 mg/day or CBD 300 mg/day; seven per group), Chagas et al. found no statistically significant differences in UPDRS scores, plasma BDNF levels or H(1)-MRS measures, while mean total PDQ-39 scores differed between the placebo and CBD 300 mg/day groups (p = 0.05); the authors write that their findings point to a possible effect of CBD in improving quality of life measures and that studies with larger samples and specific objectives are required before definitive conclusions can be drawn. (low confidence) — https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/25237116/ · keywords: Parkinson's disease rehabilitation and adjunct therapies: exercise, physical, speech and occupational therapy, dance, music, acupuncture, cannabis and supplements
- [statement] In the Duncan and Earhart randomized trial, 62 participants were assigned to a twice-weekly community-based Argentine tango program or a no-intervention control group and assessed off anti-Parkinson medication; on the primary MDS-UPDRS-3 outcome the control group showed no significant change over 12 months whereas the tango group had a reduction of 28.7% (12.8 points), and the authors suggest that long-term participation in tango may modify progression of disability in PD. (medium confidence) — https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/21959675/ · keywords: Parkinson's disease rehabilitation and adjunct therapies: exercise, physical, speech and occupational therapy, dance, music, acupuncture, cannabis and supplements · also: https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7406058/
- [statement] For balance training the APTA clinical practice guideline states evidence quality high and recommendation strength strong; the Cochrane network meta-analysis reports that gait/balance/functional training probably has a moderate beneficial effect on the severity of motor signs (MD -7.50, 95% CI -11.39 to -3.48; moderate confidence; negative estimates reflect improvement); and a physiotherapy meta-analysis of 191 trials reports that balance and gait training, among other modalities, improved motor symptoms, balance, and gait. (high confidence) — https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9046970/ · keywords: Parkinson's disease rehabilitation and adjunct therapies: exercise, physical, speech and occupational therapy, dance, music, acupuncture, cannabis and supplements · also: https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11001292/, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7564288/
- [statement] For flexibility exercises the APTA clinical practice guideline states evidence quality low and recommendation strength weak, noting that the evidence quality was rated low because there was only 1 study of moderate quality that met the inclusion criteria; the Cochrane network meta-analysis reports that the evidence is very uncertain about the effect of flexibility training on the severity of motor signs (MD 4.20, 95% CI -1.61 to 9.92; very low confidence). (medium confidence) — https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9046970/ · keywords: Parkinson's disease rehabilitation and adjunct therapies: exercise, physical, speech and occupational therapy, dance, music, acupuncture, cannabis and supplements · also: https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11001292/
- [statement] In the PD REHAB multicenter, open-label randomized trial in the United Kingdom (762 patients with mild to moderate PD; 381 randomized to physiotherapy and occupational therapy and 381 to no therapy), there was no difference between groups at 3 months in the primary outcome, the Nottingham Extended Activities of Daily Living score (difference 0.5 points; 95% CI -0.7 to 1.7), and the authors concluded that the evidence does not support the use of low-dose, patient-centered, goal-directed physiotherapy and occupational therapy in patients in the early stages of PD; the NIHR Health Technology Assessment report of the same trial concluded that NHS physiotherapy and occupational therapy did not produce immediate or long-term clinically meaningful improvements in ADL or quality of life. (medium confidence) — https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/26785394/ · keywords: Parkinson's disease rehabilitation and adjunct therapies: exercise, physical, speech and occupational therapy, dance, music, acupuncture, cannabis and supplements · also: https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC5018686/
- [statement] The PD COMM authors report that the trial could not be blinded, that outcomes were questionnaires completed by participants or carers (with possible performance bias), and that recruitment closed at 388 of 546 planned participants (71% of target) after the covid-19 pandemic; the NIHR report likewise states that recruitment did not meet the pre-specified power, and Parkinson's UK commented that the findings may be less clear-cut than they first appear because NHS speech and language therapy varies widely and there is no consensus on what 'standard' therapy is. (medium confidence) — https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11232530/ · keywords: Parkinson's disease rehabilitation and adjunct therapies: exercise, physical, speech and occupational therapy, dance, music, acupuncture, cannabis and supplements · also: https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11474952/, https://www.parkinsons.org.uk/news/2024/results-major-study-speech-and-language-therapy-parkinsons-published
- [statement] Reported effects of LSVT LOUD on speech intelligibility are mixed: RCSLT guidance (last updated December 2025) says eight studies reported improvement and two did not, depending on how intelligibility was measured; the Cochrane review comparing therapy techniques (searches up to April 2011) says all included trials assessed intelligibility and almost all results were not statistically significant; and a meta-analysis by Pu and colleagues reported pooled speech intelligibility of 16.54 (95% CI 11.35-21.72) with heterogeneity of 77%. (medium confidence) (verified as of 2026-11-27) — https://www.rcslt.org/members/clinical-guidance/parkinsons/parkinsons-guidance/ · keywords: Parkinson's disease rehabilitation and adjunct therapies: exercise, physical, speech and occupational therapy, dance, music, acupuncture, cannabis and supplements · also: https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7120320/, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8782619/
- [statement] In the NINDS NET-PD program, a randomized phase II futility trial of creatine and minocycline (Neurology 2006) found that neither could be rejected as futile and recommended considering both for definitive phase III trials, whereas the later Long-term Study 1 of creatine monohydrate 10 g/d (JAMA 2015; 1741 participants) was terminated early for futility at a planned interim analysis (n = 955) and concluded that creatine did not improve clinical outcomes. (high confidence) — https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/16481597/ · keywords: Parkinson's disease rehabilitation and adjunct therapies: exercise, physical, speech and occupational therapy, dance, music, acupuncture, cannabis and supplements · also: https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4349346/, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC13442935/
- [statement] Two analyses of commercial Mucuna pruriens products reported wide variation in levodopa content: a 2018 HPLC analysis of six products found levodopa content varying from 6% to 141% of label claims with no product within the 90%–110% pharmacopeial limits, and a 2022 JAMA Neurology case series of 16 analyzed supplements found 15 containing levodopa at 2 mg to 241 mg per recommended serving, with actual levodopa 228% to 2186% greater than the estimate for products listing a seed-extract quantity, while carbidopa and benserazide were not detected. (high confidence) — https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC5808387/ · keywords: Parkinson's disease rehabilitation and adjunct therapies: exercise, physical, speech and occupational therapy, dance, music, acupuncture, cannabis and supplements · also: https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9361182/

## Problems, failure modes and limitations

- [statement] Two systematic reviews found no significant advantage of acupuncture over placebo acupuncture on the Unified Parkinson's Disease Rating Scale (UPDRS): the Lee et al. review in Movement Disorders (eleven RCTs) pooled three placebo-controlled RCTs (n = 96, WMD, 5.7; 95% CI -2.8 to 14.2, P = 0.19) and judged the evidence 'not convincing', and the Noh et al. meta-analysis (42 studies involving 2625 participants) reported that its results failed to show acupuncture significantly more effective than placebo acupuncture in total UPDRS. (high confidence) — https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/18618661/ · keywords: Parkinson's disease rehabilitation and adjunct therapies: exercise, physical, speech and occupational therapy, dance, music, acupuncture, cannabis and supplements · also: https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/28917379/
- [statement] In Yan et al., a single-center double-blind RCT in China that randomized people with PD and sleep complaints to real or sham acupuncture for 4 weeks (83 enrolled, 78 analyzed), Parkinson Disease Sleep Scale (PDSS) scores rose more with real than sham acupuncture after 4 weeks of treatment (19.75; 95% CI 11.02-28.49; P < .001), while the authors report that no statistically significant improvements in motor symptoms and daytime sleepiness were observed among the secondary outcomes. (medium confidence) — https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11208974/ · keywords: Parkinson's disease rehabilitation and adjunct therapies: exercise, physical, speech and occupational therapy, dance, music, acupuncture, cannabis and supplements · also: https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC13189933/
- [statement] Trial reports and reviews state that acupuncturists cannot be blinded and that the evidence base is geographically concentrated: Yan et al. note the nature of acupuncture resulted in the acupuncturists being unblinded; Cui et al. state that acupuncturists could not be blinded, that the evidence base is small and predominantly from China, and that the predominance of positive findings raises the possibility that effects may be overestimated if negative or null trials remain unpublished; and Yu et al. state that full double-blinding was rarely feasible and allocation concealment was often inadequately reported. (high confidence) — https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11208974/ · keywords: Parkinson's disease rehabilitation and adjunct therapies: exercise, physical, speech and occupational therapy, dance, music, acupuncture, cannabis and supplements · also: https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC13189933/, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12488745/
- [statement] Evidence-quality statements on massage in PD are cautious: Kang et al. report approximately 42.9% low risk, 42.9% some concerns and 14.3% high risk of overall bias and note that complete blinding of participants and personnel was impossible; Angelopoulou et al. cite methodological concerns, say longitudinal studies are needed, and report that Yin Tui Na technique combined with acupuncture was associated with worse motor scores; and Parkinson's UK says research suggests massage may help to reduce pain, anxiety and depression, although there is no conclusive evidence. (high confidence) (verified as of 2026-11-27) — https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9483027/ · keywords: Parkinson's disease rehabilitation and adjunct therapies: exercise, physical, speech and occupational therapy, dance, music, acupuncture, cannabis and supplements · also: https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/32147033/, https://www.parkinsons.org.uk/information/treatments/complementary-therapies
- [statement] NICE guideline NG71 (published 19 July 2017) recommendation 1.7.4 reads 'Consider the Alexander Technique for people with Parkinson's disease who are experiencing balance or motor function problems', and Parkinson's UK states that NICE clinical guidelines recommend that people with Parkinson's consider the Alexander technique to help with balance or motor problems (a page whose footer says 'Last updated November 2018'). (high confidence) (verified as of 2026-11-27) — https://www.nice.org.uk/guidance/ng71/chapter/Recommendations · keywords: Parkinson's disease rehabilitation and adjunct therapies: exercise, physical, speech and occupational therapy, dance, music, acupuncture, cannabis and supplements · also: https://www.parkinsons.org.uk/information/treatments/complementary-therapies
- [statement] Parkinson's UK states that there is little scientific evidence that complementary therapies can slow, stop or reverse the development of Parkinson's and that it does not endorse any particular therapies, while the Parkinson's Foundation says some therapies have even shown promise in Parkinson's studies but research is still in the initial stages and that acupuncture is also sometimes used to alleviate PD pain. (medium confidence) (verified as of 2026-11-27) — https://www.parkinsons.org.uk/information/treatments/complementary-therapies · keywords: Parkinson's disease rehabilitation and adjunct therapies: exercise, physical, speech and occupational therapy, dance, music, acupuncture, cannabis and supplements · also: https://www.parkinson.org/blog/awareness/complementary-therapies
- [statement] In the Colorado phase 2 randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial of oral CBD/THC in PD (61 randomized: 31 CBD/THC, 30 placebo; final dose of 2.5mg/kg/day), motor MDS-UPDRS was reduced by 4.57 with CBD/THC and 2.77 with placebo and the between-group difference was not significant (-1.80, p = 0.379); the registry record NCT03582137, which gives the same enrollment window (9/5/2018 to 1/4/2022) and the same 61 randomized, posts a net mean difference of -1.8049 and p = 0.3785; the authors report that sleep, cognition and activities of daily living showed a treatment effect favoring placebo, and conclude that the brief duration and strong placebo response limit interpretation but there was no benefit, perhaps worsened cognition and sleep, and many mild adverse events. (medium confidence) — https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11102313/ · keywords: Parkinson's disease rehabilitation and adjunct therapies: exercise, physical, speech and occupational therapy, dance, music, acupuncture, cannabis and supplements · also: https://clinicaltrials.gov/study/NCT03582137
- [statement] As published, the Parkinson's Foundation consensus statement (May 2020) says that, given the lack of any clear data supporting the use of cannabis in PD, the Foundation does not endorse its use for PD symptoms or to modify disease progression; the Foundation's web page states that there is no conclusive evidence marijuana helps with PD symptoms; and a document hosted on the Michael J. Fox Foundation website, with content current to March 2022, states that controlled trials have not yet proven the safety or benefit of cannabis in Parkinson's. (high confidence) (verified as of 2026-11-27) — https://www.parkinson.org/sites/default/files/documents/medical_cannabis_statement_finalv2_5.pdf · keywords: Parkinson's disease rehabilitation and adjunct therapies: exercise, physical, speech and occupational therapy, dance, music, acupuncture, cannabis and supplements · also: https://www.parkinson.org/living-with-parkinsons/treatment/medical-marijuana, https://www.michaeljfox.org/sites/default/files/media/document/Medical_Marijuana_03.04.22.pdf
- [statement] The 2014 American Academy of Neurology systematic review of medical marijuana in selected neurologic disorders concluded that oral cannabis extract is probably ineffective for treating levodopa-induced dyskinesias in patients with Parkinson disease; the PubMed record title of this report carries the label [RETIRED], and the Parkinson's Foundation 2020 statement cites the same AAN conclusion. (medium confidence) (verified as of 2026-11-27) — https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/24778283/ · keywords: Parkinson's disease rehabilitation and adjunct therapies: exercise, physical, speech and occupational therapy, dance, music, acupuncture, cannabis and supplements · also: https://www.parkinson.org/sites/default/files/documents/medical_cannabis_statement_finalv2_5.pdf
- [statement] The APTA clinical practice guideline for physical therapist management of Parkinson disease states that physical therapists should recommend community-based exercise to reduce motor disease severity and improve nonmotor symptoms, functional outcomes, and quality of life, rating evidence strength as high and recommendation strength as strong. (high confidence) (verified as of 2026-11-27) — https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9046970/ · keywords: Parkinson's disease rehabilitation and adjunct therapies: exercise, physical, speech and occupational therapy, dance, music, acupuncture, cannabis and supplements · also: https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11687919/
- [statement] In the Li et al. randomized trial (NCT00611481), 195 patients with Hoehn and Yahr stage 1 to 4 Parkinson's disease were assigned to tai chi, resistance training or stretching for 60-minute sessions twice weekly for 24 weeks, and the tai chi group performed better than the resistance-training and stretching groups on the primary outcome of maximum excursion (between-group differences of 5.55 and 11.98 percentage points) and on directional control (10.45 and 11.38 percentage points). (medium confidence) — https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3285459/ · keywords: Parkinson's disease rehabilitation and adjunct therapies: exercise, physical, speech and occupational therapy, dance, music, acupuncture, cannabis and supplements · also: https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC5618798/
- [statement] Meta-analytic findings on tai chi and qigong and quality of life in Parkinson's disease differ: Song et al. (15 RCTs) reported improved quality of life (ES=-0.393, p<.001), whereas a meta-analysis of seven systematic reviews (Fidan et al.) and a meta-analysis of thirteen RCTs of traditional Chinese exercises (Song et al., later version) reported no statistically significant quality-of-life effect. (medium confidence) — https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC5618798/ · keywords: Parkinson's disease rehabilitation and adjunct therapies: exercise, physical, speech and occupational therapy, dance, music, acupuncture, cannabis and supplements · also: https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/31116118/, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12847013/
- [statement] Review authors state quality limits on the dance literature: an umbrella review of 55 systematic reviews rated the overall confidence in the results of 38 reviews (69%) as critically low; a systematic review of 20 RCTs (N = 723) reported that small samples and methodological limitations resulted in low-certainty evidence across outcomes; and a systematic review of sixteen RCTs noted that performance bias cannot be controlled because participants and personnel cannot be blinded to a dance intervention and that less than half of the studies used a low-risk randomization procedure. (high confidence) — https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11687919/ · keywords: Parkinson's disease rehabilitation and adjunct therapies: exercise, physical, speech and occupational therapy, dance, music, acupuncture, cannabis and supplements · also: https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8456607/, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7406058/
- [statement] Systematic reviews of boxing for Parkinson's disease differ: Wang et al. (13 studies, 402 patients, pre-post assessments of boxing interventions) conclude that boxing exercise can effectively improve both motor and non-motor symptoms with safety and high adherence, whereas Gonzalez-Devesa et al. (13 studies) report no significant pooled effect on functional mobility, balance, motor symptoms, gait and cardiorespiratory fitness and call the evidence uncertain, and Hernandez-Martinez et al. (eight studies, 100 older people) conclude that boxing does not significantly improve balance, cardiorespiratory fitness and health-related quality of life. (medium confidence) — https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11983467/ · keywords: Parkinson's disease rehabilitation and adjunct therapies: exercise, physical, speech and occupational therapy, dance, music, acupuncture, cannabis and supplements · also: https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11778260/, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12179875/, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6904341/
- [statement] Meta-analyses of yoga in Parkinson's disease report benefit with caveats about robustness: Ban et al. (ten studies, 359 participants) report better motor status (MD = −5.64) with yoga and state that their results should be interpreted with caution, Suárez-Iglesias et al. report that a meta-analysis on five RCTs found yoga more effective than passive control for motor symptoms, whereas a network meta-analysis of mind-body exercises (Bai et al.) found that the significant effects of yoga did not prove robust in sensitivity analysis. (medium confidence) — https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8275425/ · keywords: Parkinson's disease rehabilitation and adjunct therapies: exercise, physical, speech and occupational therapy, dance, music, acupuncture, cannabis and supplements · also: https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/34533097/, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC13751929/
- [statement] Systematic reviews of Nordic walking in Parkinson's disease differ in how they characterize benefit: Salse-Batán et al. (twelve studies) report that none of the statistically significant benefits were clinically meaningful except for walking ability and that Nordic Walking does not lead to clinically significant changes in global motor impairment, functional mobility, balance and physical fitness, whereas De Santis and Kaplan (13 studies, 318 patients) report that symptom severity, walking speed and gait pattern consistently improved after 4 to 24 weeks of Nordic walking relative to baseline or any control condition during ON-phases of pharmacotherapy, while rating study quality as poor to moderate. (medium confidence) — https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/35593147/ · keywords: Parkinson's disease rehabilitation and adjunct therapies: exercise, physical, speech and occupational therapy, dance, music, acupuncture, cannabis and supplements · also: https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/32507150/
- [statement] NICE guideline NG71 (published 19 July 2017; its overview page states last reviewed 19 December 2024) recommends offering Parkinson's disease-specific physiotherapy to people experiencing balance or motor function problems (recommendation 1.7.3) and considering referral of people in the early stages to a physiotherapist with experience of Parkinson's disease (recommendation 1.7.2); the 2024 German Society for Neurology guideline states that people with PD and impairment from motor symptoms in everyday life should have access to physiotherapy treatment. (medium confidence) (verified as of 2026-11-27) — https://www.nice.org.uk/guidance/ng71/chapter/Recommendations · keywords: Parkinson's disease rehabilitation and adjunct therapies: exercise, physical, speech and occupational therapy, dance, music, acupuncture, cannabis and supplements · also: https://www.nice.org.uk/guidance/ng71, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11157782/
- [statement] The Cochrane network meta-analysis of 154 RCTs (7837 participants, mostly mild to moderate disease) found little evidence of differences between exercise types and noted that the exact exercise type might be secondary; the earlier Cochrane physiotherapy review reported no evidence that the treatment effect differed across physiotherapy interventions (based on indirect comparisons), and the APTA guideline states that its aerobic exercise studies suggest no single form of aerobic exercise was superior to another. (medium confidence) — https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11001292/ · keywords: Parkinson's disease rehabilitation and adjunct therapies: exercise, physical, speech and occupational therapy, dance, music, acupuncture, cannabis and supplements · also: https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7120224/, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9046970/
- [statement] Sources differ in how firmly they describe exercise as slowing PD progression: the Parkinson's Foundation exercise page and a physiotherapy review state progression-related benefits (slowed symptom progression, a potential neuroprotective effect, delayed disability), whereas the APTA guideline, a review by Crotty and Schwarzschild and the SPARX3 protocol describe whether exercise modifies disease progression as an open question. (medium confidence) (verified as of 2026-11-27) — https://www.parkinson.org/living-with-parkinsons/treatment/exercise · keywords: Parkinson's disease rehabilitation and adjunct therapies: exercise, physical, speech and occupational therapy, dance, music, acupuncture, cannabis and supplements · also: https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11382789/, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9046970/, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7318912/, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9535216/
- [statement] Adverse-event statements in the sources include the following: the Cochrane network meta-analysis states that the evidence is very uncertain about the effect of physical exercise on the risk of adverse events (very low confidence), with falls (18 studies) and pain (10 studies) the most frequently reported events; the APTA guideline reports minor musculoskeletal injuries in some aerobic exercise studies, most of which resolved without incident; the SPARX phase 2 trial reported that anticipated adverse musculoskeletal events were not severe; and PD REHAB reported no difference in adverse events. (medium confidence) — https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11001292/ · keywords: Parkinson's disease rehabilitation and adjunct therapies: exercise, physical, speech and occupational therapy, dance, music, acupuncture, cannabis and supplements · also: https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9046970/, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC5838616/, https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/26785394/
- [statement] Reviews state limits in trial quality: the Cochrane physiotherapy review considered the trials to be at a mixed risk of bias and said the quality of most included trials was not high; the physiotherapy meta-analysis by Radder and colleagues stated that methodological quality and reporting was highly variable and often inadequate and that most trials had relatively small sample sizes; and the Cochrane network meta-analysis reported that confidence in the effects ranged from moderate to very low, that studies were very small, and that larger, well-conducted studies are needed. (medium confidence) — https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7120224/ · keywords: Parkinson's disease rehabilitation and adjunct therapies: exercise, physical, speech and occupational therapy, dance, music, acupuncture, cannabis and supplements · also: https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7564288/, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11001292/
- [statement] In PD COMM, a pragmatic, UK-based, unblinded, three-arm randomised trial of 388 people with Parkinson's disease and dysarthria, the primary outcome (self-reported Voice Handicap Index total score at three months, where a low score is positive) was lower with LSVT LOUD than with no speech and language therapy (-8.0 points; 99% confidence interval -13.3 to -2.6; P<0.001) and lower than with NHS speech and language therapy (-9.6 points; -14.9 to -4.4). (medium confidence) — https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11232530/ · keywords: Parkinson's disease rehabilitation and adjunct therapies: exercise, physical, speech and occupational therapy, dance, music, acupuncture, cannabis and supplements · also: https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11474952/
- [statement] In PD COMM, the Voice Handicap Index total score remained lower with LSVT LOUD than with no speech and language therapy at six months (-7.2; 99% confidence interval -13.3 to -1.1) and at 12 months (-6.7; -12.6 to -0.8); the authors write that re-intervention might still be required should the treatment effect wear off or as Parkinson's disease progresses. (medium confidence) — https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11232530/ · keywords: Parkinson's disease rehabilitation and adjunct therapies: exercise, physical, speech and occupational therapy, dance, music, acupuncture, cannabis and supplements · also: https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11474952/
- [statement] In a randomized controlled trial funded by the National Institutes of Health and LSVT Global, Inc. (several authors report employment or consulting roles with LSVT Global), 64 participants with Parkinson's disease were randomized to LSVT LOUD, LSVT ARTIC or no treatment; sound pressure level (the primary outcome) improved more with LSVT LOUD than with LSVT ARTIC or no treatment at 1 and 7 months, while between-group differences in the participant-reported CETI-M were not significant at 7 months (P = 0.08). (low confidence) — https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6261685/ · keywords: Parkinson's disease rehabilitation and adjunct therapies: exercise, physical, speech and occupational therapy, dance, music, acupuncture, cannabis and supplements
- [statement] NICE guideline NG71, published 19 July 2017 and last reviewed 19 December 2024, recommends offering speech and language therapy to people with Parkinson's disease who are experiencing problems with communication, swallowing or saliva (recommendation 1.7.8), including strategies to improve speech and communication 'such as attention to effort therapies'; Parkinson's UK's summary of the NICE guideline and the Canadian guideline for Parkinson disease (which grades the recommendation A and cites NICE as its source) restate it. (high confidence) (verified as of 2026-11-27) — https://www.nice.org.uk/guidance/ng71/chapter/Recommendations · keywords: Parkinson's disease rehabilitation and adjunct therapies: exercise, physical, speech and occupational therapy, dance, music, acupuncture, cannabis and supplements · also: https://www.nice.org.uk/guidance/ng71, https://www.parkinsons.org.uk/information/healthcare/nice-guidelines, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6733687/
- [statement] Two speech-therapy guidance documents name LSVT: the Royal College of Speech and Language Therapists' Parkinson's guidance (last updated December 2025) states that LSVT LOUD is highly recommended for communication problems in people with Parkinson's, calls it the only behavioural treatment with strong evidence for managing dysarthria (supported by 40 studies), and recommends telehealth in specific well-defined treatments such as LSVT LOUD; the Dutch guideline for speech-language therapy in Parkinson's disease (Dutch text published in 2008; English edition copyright 2011) strongly recommends PLVT or LSVT for people with hypokinetic dysarthria who satisfy the indications for intensive treatment. (medium confidence) (verified as of 2026-11-27) — https://www.rcslt.org/members/clinical-guidance/parkinsons/parkinsons-guidance/ · keywords: Parkinson's disease rehabilitation and adjunct therapies: exercise, physical, speech and occupational therapy, dance, music, acupuncture, cannabis and supplements · also: https://www.parkinsonnet.nl/app/uploads/sites/3/2019/11/dutch_slp_guidelines-final.pdf
- [statement] In a systematic review and meta-analysis of LSVT-BIG (searched to September 2017; three randomised trials of 84 participants with mild Parkinson's disease), UPDRS part III improved more than with physiotherapy exercises or a shorter training protocol (mean difference -3.20; 95% CI -5.18 to -1.23), whereas Timed Up and Go (-0.47; 95% CI -0.99 to 0.06) and 10-metre walk (-0.53; 95% CI -1.07 to 0.01) showed only trends, and the authors call this preliminary, moderate quality evidence; a separate gait-exercise meta-analysis (Ni and colleagues) described the LSVT program as yielding only a trend toward increased walking speed. (medium confidence) — https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/28980476/ · keywords: Parkinson's disease rehabilitation and adjunct therapies: exercise, physical, speech and occupational therapy, dance, music, acupuncture, cannabis and supplements · also: https://journals.sagepub.com/doi/full/10.1177/1545968318801558
- [statement] Five systematic reviews with meta-analysis of rhythmic auditory cueing, rhythmic auditory stimulation (RAS) or music-based interventions in Parkinson's disease (Ghai, Ye, Wang, Lee and Ko, and Li) each report a positive pooled effect on gait velocity or speed and on stride or step length. (high confidence) — https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC5764963/ · keywords: Parkinson's disease rehabilitation and adjunct therapies: exercise, physical, speech and occupational therapy, dance, music, acupuncture, cannabis and supplements · also: https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9366143/, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9053573/, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9859027/, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12580135/
- [statement] The Ye, Wang, Lee and Ko, and Li meta-analyses each report no statistically significant pooled effect of RAS or music-based interventions on cadence in Parkinson's disease. (high confidence) — https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9366143/ · keywords: Parkinson's disease rehabilitation and adjunct therapies: exercise, physical, speech and occupational therapy, dance, music, acupuncture, cannabis and supplements · also: https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9053573/, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9859027/, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12580135/
- [statement] Meta-analyses of RAS and music-based interventions in Parkinson's disease differ on balance and timed up-and-go (TUG) mobility: Wang and colleagues and Lee and Ko report statistically significant pooled improvements (Berg Balance Scale and TUG for Wang and colleagues; TUG for Lee and Ko), whereas Ye and colleagues report no significant pooled difference for either, and Li and colleagues report a pooled balance effect that became nonsignificant after sensitivity analysis. (high confidence) — https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9053573/ · keywords: Parkinson's disease rehabilitation and adjunct therapies: exercise, physical, speech and occupational therapy, dance, music, acupuncture, cannabis and supplements · also: https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9859027/, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9366143/, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12580135/
- [statement] Meta-analyses differ on UPDRS motor scores and freezing of gait for music-based therapy and RAS in Parkinson's disease: one meta-analysis (K = 6 studies, total N = 168) found no significant effects for UPDRS-motor score or Freezing of Gait, whereas Ye and colleagues (18 studies) report significant pooled improvements in UPDRS-III and in the Freezing of Gait Questionnaire. (high confidence) — https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/22166406/ · keywords: Parkinson's disease rehabilitation and adjunct therapies: exercise, physical, speech and occupational therapy, dance, music, acupuncture, cannabis and supplements · also: https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9366143/
- [statement] Authors of RAS and music-based meta-analyses in Parkinson's disease state evidence-quality limits themselves: Ye and colleagues note that only two included studies had more than 100 subjects and thirteen had fewer than 50; Wang and colleagues report that lack of blinding of participants and trainers was the most common risk of bias, with twelve studies at high risk for this reason, and that the largest included study had 90 participants; Lee and Ko state that allocation concealment and blinding were not possible in most trials because of the nature of the music-related activities; and Li and colleagues rated the overall methodological quality of the included RCTs as moderate. (high confidence) — https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9366143/ · keywords: Parkinson's disease rehabilitation and adjunct therapies: exercise, physical, speech and occupational therapy, dance, music, acupuncture, cannabis and supplements · also: https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9053573/, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9859027/, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12580135/
- [statement] Meta-analyses differ on non-motor outcomes of music-based or arts-based interventions in Parkinson's disease: Lee and Ko report no significant pooled effect on quality of life (SMD = −0.68, p = 0.18), and Liu and colleagues' meta-analysis of 22 studies (928 participants) reports non-significant effects on quality of life, cognition and depressive symptoms, whereas a music-therapy meta-analysis of thirty-three studies including 3635 patients (searched from inception to 31 August 2026) reports significant improvements in depression, anxiety and life quality. (medium confidence) (verified as of 2026-11-27) — https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9859027/ · keywords: Parkinson's disease rehabilitation and adjunct therapies: exercise, physical, speech and occupational therapy, dance, music, acupuncture, cannabis and supplements · also: https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC13281054/, https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/43076026/
- [statement] A systematic review of randomized controlled trials of music-based interventions for cognitive rehabilitation in Parkinson's disease, which analyzed three articles, concluded that the results showed no evidence of efficacy for cognitive outcomes, and a randomized trial of a group-based music intervention that enrolled forty-six patients (Pohl and colleagues) states that it does not support efficacy for immediate or lasting gains in dual-tasking, cognition, balance, or freezing of gait. (medium confidence) — https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10415237/ · keywords: Parkinson's disease rehabilitation and adjunct therapies: exercise, physical, speech and occupational therapy, dance, music, acupuncture, cannabis and supplements · also: https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7132435/
- [statement] Trinchillo and colleagues' review states that Butala and colleagues found significant improvements in motor functions after 24 weeks in a randomized crossover trial of weekly group singing, whereas Butala and colleagues' own Parkinsonics trial report states a significant overall-cohort MDS-UPDRS Part III improvement at 24 weeks (Δ = 5.9 points) that became nonsignificant when the baseline was adjusted in mixed linear model analyses, and that they cannot conclusively attribute motor improvements to the singing intervention. (medium confidence) — https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC13731696/ · keywords: Parkinson's disease rehabilitation and adjunct therapies: exercise, physical, speech and occupational therapy, dance, music, acupuncture, cannabis and supplements · also: https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9553721/
- [statement] Two recent systematic reviews of singing in Parkinson's disease word their conclusions differently: Irons and Sheffield (23 studies, 540 participants; last search 3 April 2025) rate the certainty of the one RCT-based favourable outcome as very low and state that, due to insufficient high-quality evidence, they are unable to determine the effects of singing interventions, whereas Trinchillo and colleagues (twenty-six studies, 1057 patients; considerable heterogeneity precluded meta-analysis) conclude that singing is a promising adjunct therapy. (high confidence) (verified as of 2026-11-27) — https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12645629/ · keywords: Parkinson's disease rehabilitation and adjunct therapies: exercise, physical, speech and occupational therapy, dance, music, acupuncture, cannabis and supplements · also: https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC13731696/
- [statement] A systematic review of active group-based performing arts interventions in Parkinson's disease (searches conducted in February 2020) included fifty-six studies reported in 67 publications with a total of 1531 people with PD; dance was studied most (38 studies), followed by 12 studies on singing, four on music therapy and two on theatrical interventions, and the authors state that no studies compared interventions from different performing arts modalities. (low confidence) — https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7547481/ · keywords: Parkinson's disease rehabilitation and adjunct therapies: exercise, physical, speech and occupational therapy, dance, music, acupuncture, cannabis and supplements
- [statement] Reviews and a patient-organisation page describe the creative-therapy evidence base in Parkinson's disease as limited by small samples and weak designs: Barnish and Barran list small sample sizes and the absence of control groups in over half of the included studies among the main methodological concerns, Irons and Sheffield report that most singing studies' methods were not rated highly due to small sample sizes, blinding and weak study design, and the American Parkinson Disease Association page states that most complementary therapies, which it lists as including singing, music therapy, dance therapy, theater and art therapy, have usually been studied only in small groups of people. (high confidence) — https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7547481/ · keywords: Parkinson's disease rehabilitation and adjunct therapies: exercise, physical, speech and occupational therapy, dance, music, acupuncture, cannabis and supplements · also: https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12645629/, https://www.apdaparkinson.org/article/music-therapy-parkinsons-disease/
- [statement] On visual-art therapy in Parkinson's disease, an observational, prospective, open-label, exploratory study of eighteen patients reported improved Navon test, eye-tracking and UPDRS performance after twenty sessions of art therapy, whereas the authors of an art-therapy meta-analysis state that visual arts and painting represent a significant research gap whose direct therapeutic effects remain unexplored. (medium confidence) — https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/33526323/ · keywords: Parkinson's disease rehabilitation and adjunct therapies: exercise, physical, speech and occupational therapy, dance, music, acupuncture, cannabis and supplements · also: https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12444631/
- [statement] NICE guideline NG71 (published 19 July 2017; its overview page records 'Last reviewed: 19 December 2024') includes recommendation 1.7.6, 'Offer Parkinson's disease-specific occupational therapy for people who are having difficulties with activities of daily living', and recommendation 1.7.5, which advises considering referral of people in the early stages of Parkinson's disease to an occupational therapist with experience of Parkinson's disease for assessment, education and advice on motor and non-motor symptoms; the 2022 American Occupational Therapy Association practice guideline states that 'Multidisciplinary, tailored, goal-oriented intervention is recommended for people with PD'. (medium confidence) (verified as of 2026-11-27) — https://www.nice.org.uk/guidance/ng71/chapter/recommendations · keywords: Parkinson's disease rehabilitation and adjunct therapies: exercise, physical, speech and occupational therapy, dance, music, acupuncture, cannabis and supplements · also: https://www.nice.org.uk/guidance/ng71, https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/35648119/
- [statement] In the OTiP multicentre, assessor-masked randomised controlled trial, 191 patients with Parkinson's disease and self-reported difficulties in daily activities were randomly assigned to 10 weeks of home-based occupational therapy (n=124) or usual care with no occupational therapy (n=67); the adjusted mean difference in Canadian Occupational Performance Measure score at 3 months was in favour of the intervention group (1·2; 95% CI 0·8-1·6; p<0·0001), and there were no adverse events associated with the study. (medium confidence) — https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/24726066/ · keywords: Parkinson's disease rehabilitation and adjunct therapies: exercise, physical, speech and occupational therapy, dance, music, acupuncture, cannabis and supplements · also: https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/25854809/
- [statement] In the PD REHAB multicenter, open-label, parallel group, controlled efficacy trial, 762 patients with mild to moderate Parkinson's disease and limitations in activities of daily living were randomized to physiotherapy and occupational therapy or no therapy; there was no difference between groups at 3 months in the primary outcome, the Nottingham Extended Activities of Daily Living scale total score (difference, 0.5 points; 95% CI, -0.7 to 1.7; P = .41), the median therapist contact time was 4 visits of 58 minutes over 8 weeks, and the authors concluded that physiotherapy and occupational therapy were not associated with immediate or medium-term clinically meaningful improvements in ADL or quality of life in mild to moderate PD. (medium confidence) — https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/26785394/ · keywords: Parkinson's disease rehabilitation and adjunct therapies: exercise, physical, speech and occupational therapy, dance, music, acupuncture, cannabis and supplements · also: https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC5018686/
- [statement] A Cochrane review of occupational therapy for Parkinson's disease, with electronic searches up to April 2007, identified two trials with 84 patients in total, and its authors concluded that there is insufficient evidence to support or refute the efficacy of occupational therapy in Parkinson's disease; the PD REHAB report describes Cochrane reviews of physiotherapy and occupational therapy for Parkinson's disease as having found insufficient evidence of effectiveness. (medium confidence) — https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6991932/ · keywords: Parkinson's disease rehabilitation and adjunct therapies: exercise, physical, speech and occupational therapy, dance, music, acupuncture, cannabis and supplements · also: https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC5018686/
- [statement] Three systematic reviews of occupational therapy-related interventions in Parkinson's disease report beneficial findings, with their authors also noting limits on the evidence base: the first (10 studies; 1343 people with Parkinson's disease and 180 caregivers) reported that interventions focussing on meaningful activities were shown to improve perceived occupational performance, and noted that few studies have identified the effectiveness of occupational therapy intervention alone; Tofani et al. (15 randomized controlled trials, 4 in the meta-analysis) reported a significant quality-of-life improvement at 2 to 3 months follow-up (mean difference of −2.08; 95% confidence interval, −2.52 to −1.64) and considered the strength of the evidence moderate because of the limited number of studies; Foster et al. (twenty-two studies) reported strong strength of evidence for physical activity levels and handwriting, moderate for IADL participation and medication adherence, and low for cognitive rehabilitation, and noted that the review is limited by the small number of studies that specifically addressed IADL function. (medium confidence) — https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/31599467/ · keywords: Parkinson's disease rehabilitation and adjunct therapies: exercise, physical, speech and occupational therapy, dance, music, acupuncture, cannabis and supplements · also: https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7604677/, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8095707/
- [statement] Three sources include cueing among their gait recommendations: the APTA clinical practice guideline states that physical therapists should implement external cueing to reduce motor disease severity and freezing of gait (FOG) and to improve gait outcomes in individuals with Parkinson disease (evidence quality: high; recommendation strength: strong), with aggregate evidence of thirteen high-quality and 16 moderate-quality studies; Keus et al. extracted cueing strategies to improve gait as one of four treatment recommendations based on evidence from more than two controlled trials; and a 2020 systematic review of physical therapy for FOG and gait impairments reports that cueing strategies (visual and auditory) reduce FOG with a good category A recommendation. (high confidence) — https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9046970/ · keywords: Parkinson's disease rehabilitation and adjunct therapies: exercise, physical, speech and occupational therapy, dance, music, acupuncture, cannabis and supplements · also: https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/17133526/, https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/31994842/
- [statement] Three systematic reviews or meta-analyses report improved gait speed or velocity with auditory cueing in Parkinson's disease: a 2013 meta-analysis of cueing studies (searches up to September 2011) reported significant improvement of velocity with auditory cueing (Hedge g=.544; 95% CI, .294-.795); Ghai et al. (50 studies, 1892 participants) reported an overall positive effect on gait velocity, stride length, and a negative effect on cadence with application of auditory cueing; and Nascimento et al. (2024; ten trials involving 309 participants) reported that walking training with auditory cueing improved walking speed by 0.09 m/s (95% CI 0.02 to 0.15) more than walking training alone, which the authors describe as low-quality evidence. (medium confidence) — https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/23127307/ · keywords: Parkinson's disease rehabilitation and adjunct therapies: exercise, physical, speech and occupational therapy, dance, music, acupuncture, cannabis and supplements · also: https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC5764963/, https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/38897907/
- [statement] Sources differ on which type of external cue performs best for gait in Parkinson's disease: a 2013 meta-analysis concluded that auditory cueing is more effective for treating gait disorders in PD, a 2026 network meta-analysis reported somatosensory and visual cues as the most effective modalities for gait velocity and stride length, and the APTA guideline states, of reductions in motor disease severity when different modes of external cueing were compared, that no one mode of external cueing is superior to another. (medium confidence) — https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/23127307/ · keywords: Parkinson's disease rehabilitation and adjunct therapies: exercise, physical, speech and occupational therapy, dance, music, acupuncture, cannabis and supplements · also: https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC13197277/, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9046970/
- [statement] Two meta-analyses report improved walking speed with treadmill training in Parkinson's disease but no improvement in cadence: the Cochrane review (18 trials, 633 participants; last searched September 2014) reported improved gait speed (MD = 0.09 m/s; 95% confidence interval (CI) 0.03 to 0.14; moderate quality of evidence) and that cadence did not improve (MD = 2.16 steps/minute; 95% CI -0.13 to 4.46; low quality of evidence), and a second meta-analysis (16 trials across Parkinson's disease and multiple sclerosis) reported improved comfortable walking velocity in Parkinson's disease (MD 0.21m/second, 95% CI 0.15 to 0.27) and that treadmill training had no effect on cadence. (high confidence) — https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9579750/ · keywords: Parkinson's disease rehabilitation and adjunct therapies: exercise, physical, speech and occupational therapy, dance, music, acupuncture, cannabis and supplements · also: https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/30876717/
- [statement] The APTA guideline states that physical therapists should implement gait training to reduce motor disease severity and improve stride length, gait speed, mobility, and balance in individuals with PD (evidence quality: high; recommendation strength: strong) and that there was no single gait training intervention that demonstrated greater improvement than other types of gait training; two randomized trials comparing robotic gait training with treadmill training each concluded that robotic gait training was not superior (one randomly allocated 30 patients to treadmill or Lokomat gait training and, at the 6-month follow-up, found no significant differences between the 2 groups, P = .53; Picelli et al. randomly assigned sixty patients with mild to moderate Parkinson's disease into three groups). (medium confidence) — https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9046970/ · keywords: Parkinson's disease rehabilitation and adjunct therapies: exercise, physical, speech and occupational therapy, dance, music, acupuncture, cannabis and supplements · also: https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/22623206/, https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/23490463/
- [statement] The APTA clinical practice guideline on physical therapist management of Parkinson disease was published in Physical Therapy (2021 Dec 28;102(4):pzab302); its page carries a correction (Phys Ther. 2022 Aug 27;102(8):pzac098) about an author's affiliation and a later Editor's Note (Physical Therapy, 2024;104:pzae031) stating that Greek and Chinese translations of the article have been provided; and the guideline states that in 5 years it will either be revised by APTA, reaffirmed, or withdrawn. (low confidence) (verified as of 2026-11-27) — https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9046970/ · keywords: Parkinson's disease rehabilitation and adjunct therapies: exercise, physical, speech and occupational therapy, dance, music, acupuncture, cannabis and supplements · also: https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9418923/, https://academic.oup.com/ptj/article-pdf/104/8/pzae031/58864662/pzae031.pdf
- [statement] Two coenzyme Q10 (CoQ10) trials in early Parkinson disease reported conflicting results: an eighty-subject dosage-ranging trial (Arch Neurol 2002) reported less functional decline at 1200 mg/d than with placebo (P =.04) and concluded that CoQ10 appears to slow deterioration pending confirmation in a larger study, while the phase III QE3 trial (600 participants; JAMA Neurol 2014) was terminated after a prespecified futility criterion was reached and showed no evidence of clinical benefit; a 2026 review suggests the discrepancies might stem from different sample sizes and study durations. (high confidence) — https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/12374491/ · keywords: Parkinson's disease rehabilitation and adjunct therapies: exercise, physical, speech and occupational therapy, dance, music, acupuncture, cannabis and supplements · also: https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/24664227/, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC13442935/
- [statement] Two published meta-analyses of randomized trials of coenzyme Q10 in Parkinson disease reported no significant benefit over placebo: a 2016 analysis of five RCTs (981 patients) found that the overall effect did not favor either group for total UPDRS, and a 2017 analysis of eight studies (899 patients) found a pooled WMD of 1.02 for UPDRS part 3 (p = 0.54) and stated that routine CoQ10 treatment of PD could not be recommended. (high confidence) — https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/26553164/ · keywords: Parkinson's disease rehabilitation and adjunct therapies: exercise, physical, speech and occupational therapy, dance, music, acupuncture, cannabis and supplements · also: https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/27830343/
- [statement] A 2014 Cochrane review (searches to 10 November 2013; two RCTs, 194 patients) reported no clear evidence of an effect of creatine on motor function (MD -0.26; 95% CI -4.39 to 3.88; low quality evidence) and judged the evidence base limited by risk of bias, small sample sizes and short duration, and a 2017 BMC Neurology meta-analysis (five RCTs, 1339 participants) reported no significant differences in total, mental, activities of daily living or motor UPDRS scores, with an improvement in Schwab & England Scale scores, and concluded that creatine has no observed benefit in PD. (high confidence) — https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10196714/ · keywords: Parkinson's disease rehabilitation and adjunct therapies: exercise, physical, speech and occupational therapy, dance, music, acupuncture, cannabis and supplements · also: https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC5457735/
- [statement] Published conclusions on isradipine in early Parkinson disease differ: the STEADY-PD III trial (336 patients; 5 mg of immediate-release isradipine twice daily or placebo for 36 months) reported that long-term treatment did not slow clinical progression (treatment effect -0.27 point, P = 0.85), whereas a re-analysis of STEADY-PD II data (10 mg/day extended-release isradipine) reported significantly smaller UPDRS scores than placebo at the end of the 52-week trial, with post hoc adjustment for symptomatic therapy diminishing the statistical significance, and suggested that clinically attainable brain exposure to isradipine may slow early-stage progression. (high confidence) — https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7465126/ · keywords: Parkinson's disease rehabilitation and adjunct therapies: exercise, physical, speech and occupational therapy, dance, music, acupuncture, cannabis and supplements · also: https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8922308/
- [statement] In a randomized trial of tocopherol (a component of vitamin E) and deprenyl in early Parkinson's disease (800 patients assigned to placebo, tocopherol, deprenyl or both; N Engl J Med 1993), there was no beneficial effect of tocopherol or any interaction between tocopherol and deprenyl, and a 2026 review likewise reports that no benefits of vitamin E were seen in UPDRS total score. (high confidence) — https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/8417384/ · keywords: Parkinson's disease rehabilitation and adjunct therapies: exercise, physical, speech and occupational therapy, dance, music, acupuncture, cannabis and supplements · also: https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC13442935/
- [statement] Reports on vitamin D supplementation and motor outcomes in Parkinson disease are mixed: a double-blind placebo-controlled trial (114 patients; vitamin D3 1200 IU/d for 12 months; Am J Clin Nutr 2013) reported that vitamin D3 significantly prevented deterioration of the Hoehn and Yahr stage (P = 0.005), a 2025 meta-analysis of 8 randomized trials (646 cases) found no reduction in UPDRS part III but a benefit on 6-Minute walking test distance, and a 2026 randomized trial (2000 IU/d for 12 weeks) reported no significant improvement in motor function; a 2026 review judged that firm conclusions on the disease-modifying potential of vitamin D cannot yet be drawn. (high confidence) (verified as of 2026-11-27) — https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/23485413/ · keywords: Parkinson's disease rehabilitation and adjunct therapies: exercise, physical, speech and occupational therapy, dance, music, acupuncture, cannabis and supplements · also: https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12183021/, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC13406316/, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC13442935/
- [statement] NICE guideline NG71 (published 19 July 2017), section 1.6 on pharmacological neuroprotective therapy, recommends against using vitamin E as a neuroprotective therapy for people with Parkinson's disease (1.6.1) and against using co-enzyme Q10 as a neuroprotective therapy except in the context of clinical trials (1.6.2), both marked as 2006, amended 2017; a 2026 review reports that CoQ10 is classified as non-efficacious for delaying progression of PD by both the International Parkinson & Movement Disorders Society and the National Institute for Health Care Excellence at the time of writing. (medium confidence) (verified as of 2026-11-27) — https://www.nice.org.uk/guidance/ng71/chapter/Recommendations · keywords: Parkinson's disease rehabilitation and adjunct therapies: exercise, physical, speech and occupational therapy, dance, music, acupuncture, cannabis and supplements · also: https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC13442935/
- [statement] NICE guideline NG71 (published 19 July 2017) recommends in 1.7.13 that people with Parkinson's disease be advised to take a vitamin D supplement, in 1.7.14 that creatine supplements not be offered to people with Parkinson's disease, and in 1.7.15 that people with Parkinson's disease be advised not to take over-the-counter dietary supplements without first consulting their pharmacist or other healthcare professional; a 2026 review distinguishes supplements used to correct deficiencies, such as vitamin D for bone health, which it places outside its scope, from supplements explored for disease-modifying potential. (medium confidence) (verified as of 2026-11-27) — https://www.nice.org.uk/guidance/ng71/chapter/Recommendations · keywords: Parkinson's disease rehabilitation and adjunct therapies: exercise, physical, speech and occupational therapy, dance, music, acupuncture, cannabis and supplements · also: https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC13442935/
- [statement] The American Academy of Neurology practice parameter on neuroprotective strategies and alternative therapies for Parkinson disease (Neurology 2006) reported the conclusions that no treatment has been shown to be neuroprotective and that there is no evidence that vitamin or food additives can improve motor function in PD; a 2026 review states that multiple phase II and III trials of pharmacological agents aimed at modulating PD pathophysiological hallmarks all failed to demonstrate significant disease-modifying effects. (medium confidence) — https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/16606908/ · keywords: Parkinson's disease rehabilitation and adjunct therapies: exercise, physical, speech and occupational therapy, dance, music, acupuncture, cannabis and supplements · also: https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC13442935/

## Comparisons and alternatives

- [statement] Meta-analyses of acupuncture combined with conventional treatment report better UPDRS results than the comparison arm while describing the evidence as limited: one meta-analysis (42 studies involving 2625 participants) found that combined acupuncture and conventional medication showed significant improvements in total UPDRS, UPDRS I, UPDRS II and UPDRS III compared with conventional medication alone and rated the methodological quality of the RCTs low, and Yu et al. (50 RCTs, n = 3,248; acupuncture modalities combined with standard PD therapy) report acupuncture significantly outperforming Western medicine across all UPDRS domains while stating that the overall certainty of evidence ranged from moderate to low across most outcomes. (high confidence) — https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/28917379/ · keywords: Parkinson's disease rehabilitation and adjunct therapies: exercise, physical, speech and occupational therapy, dance, music, acupuncture, cannabis and supplements · also: https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12488745/
- [statement] In a three-group RCT in ninety-three people with idiopathic PD (24 lessons in the Alexander Technique, 24 sessions of massage, or no additional intervention), the Alexander Technique group improved compared with the no additional intervention group on the Self-assessment Parkinson's Disease Disability Scale at best (p = 0.04) and at worst (p = 0.01), with the comparative improvement maintained at six-month follow-up; a systematic review of Alexander Technique lessons (Woodman and Moore) concluded there was moderate evidence in Parkinson's-associated disability, and Parkinson's UK describes the evidence as one study of fewer than 100 people. (medium confidence) (verified as of 2026-11-27) — https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/12428818/ · keywords: Parkinson's disease rehabilitation and adjunct therapies: exercise, physical, speech and occupational therapy, dance, music, acupuncture, cannabis and supplements · also: https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/22171910/, https://www.parkinsons.org.uk/information/treatments/complementary-therapies
- [statement] Sources differ on electroacupuncture added to anti-parkinsonian drug therapy: the Cho et al. guideline reports that in three RCTs electroacupuncture and anti-parkinsonian drugs, compared with drug therapy alone, showed no significant difference in overall clinical effectiveness and grades it 'may be considered' (strength C, level of evidence low), whereas Yu et al., in an analysis of 50 RCTs (n = 3,248), report that among all modalities electroacupuncture showed the highest overall efficacy. (medium confidence) (verified as of 2026-11-27) — https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6196228/ · keywords: Parkinson's disease rehabilitation and adjunct therapies: exercise, physical, speech and occupational therapy, dance, music, acupuncture, cannabis and supplements · also: https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12488745/
- [statement] Adverse-event findings reported for cannabinoids versus placebo in PD include: the Fernandes et al. meta-analysis of seven randomized trials reports increased risk of confusion (risk ratio, 4.44; 95% confidence interval, 1.17-16.87) and dizziness (risk ratio, 2.78; 95% confidence interval, 1.65-4.68); the Colorado CBD/THC trial reports twice as many treatment emergent adverse events in the CBD/THC group, most of them mild; and the São Paulo cannabis-oil trial reports irritability more frequent in the CBD/THC group (P = 0.005). (medium confidence) — https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/42966680/ · keywords: Parkinson's disease rehabilitation and adjunct therapies: exercise, physical, speech and occupational therapy, dance, music, acupuncture, cannabis and supplements · also: https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11102313/, https://movementdisorders.onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/10.1002/mds.70449
- [statement] In Kubota et al. (Movement Disorders, first published 07 August 2026), a phase II randomized, placebo-controlled trial of an oral cannabis oil in PD patients with chronic pain (final daily dosage 43.88 mg CBD and 0.96 mg THC over 9 weeks; 101 randomized, 87 completed), the authors report no significant difference between CBD/THC and placebo in PD-PCS scores (P = 0.757) or in other non-motor scales, and the study was stopped due to futility after a pre-planned interim analysis; the authors conclude that the cannabis oil formulation did not improve pain or other non-motor symptoms compared with placebo. (low confidence) — https://movementdisorders.onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/10.1002/mds.70449 · keywords: Parkinson's disease rehabilitation and adjunct therapies: exercise, physical, speech and occupational therapy, dance, music, acupuncture, cannabis and supplements
- [statement] Randomized trials report different results for non-motor symptoms in PD: Peball et al. (phase II enriched-enrollment randomized withdrawal trial of nabilone; 47 patients began open-label titration and 19 patients received nabilone or placebo) reported a MDS-UPDRS-I difference of 1.63 (95% CI 0.09 to 3.18, p = 0.030) at week 4 and interpret this as potential efficacy of nabilone, with one author an employee of the study-drug manufacturer; Kubota et al. (CBD/THC oil versus placebo) reported no significant differences in other non-motor scales; and the Messak et al. meta-analysis found non-motor symptoms not significantly improved (SMD= -0.03, p = 0.94). (medium confidence) — https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/32757413/ · keywords: Parkinson's disease rehabilitation and adjunct therapies: exercise, physical, speech and occupational therapy, dance, music, acupuncture, cannabis and supplements · also: https://movementdisorders.onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/10.1002/mds.70449, https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/42138778/
- [statement] A meta-analysis of tai chi and qigong trials (Song et al.; 15 RCTs, 755 subjects) reported improvement in UPDRS III (ES=-0.444) and balance (ES=0.544), rated methodological bias low in 6 studies, moderate in 7 and high in 2, and noted that funnel plots suggested some degree of publication bias; a later meta-analysis of traditional Chinese exercises (thirteen RCTs, 859 patients) reported UPDRS-III MD -4.30 and Berg Balance Scale MD 2.63 versus usual control and noted that only one included study used a double-blind procedure. (medium confidence) — https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC5618798/ · keywords: Parkinson's disease rehabilitation and adjunct therapies: exercise, physical, speech and occupational therapy, dance, music, acupuncture, cannabis and supplements · also: https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12847013/
- [statement] Reviews report improved motor-severity scores for exercise or physiotherapy versus control: the Cochrane physiotherapy review (39 trials, 1827 participants) reported a UPDRS motor difference of -5.01 points (95% CI -6.30 to -3.72); the Cochrane network meta-analysis reported mean differences of -5.76 for endurance training and -4.96 for strength/resistance training, both rated low confidence, with a stated minimum clinically important difference of -2.5; and a meta-analysis of 18 aerobic-exercise trials (901 patients) reported a standardised mean difference of -0.57 for motor actions. (medium confidence) — https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7120224/ · keywords: Parkinson's disease rehabilitation and adjunct therapies: exercise, physical, speech and occupational therapy, dance, music, acupuncture, cannabis and supplements · also: https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11001292/, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4077570/
- [statement] Sources differ on whether high-intensity aerobic exercise gives greater motor benefit than moderate intensity: the SPARX phase 2 trial found that only its high-intensity treadmill arm reached a predefined nonfutility threshold, whereas a systematic review of vigorous-intensity aerobic exercise found no statistically significant differences versus moderate or low intensity and called the evidence too limited to allow recommendations for clinical practice. (medium confidence) — https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC5838616/ · keywords: Parkinson's disease rehabilitation and adjunct therapies: exercise, physical, speech and occupational therapy, dance, music, acupuncture, cannabis and supplements · also: https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/32978867/, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9046970/
- [statement] The PD COMM pilot trial reported a trend to improvement in the Voice Handicap Index at three months with both LSVT LOUD and standard speech and language therapy versus control, whereas the full PD COMM trial reported benefit for LSVT LOUD but no evidence of benefit for NHS speech and language therapy versus no therapy. (medium confidence) — https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC5763537/ · keywords: Parkinson's disease rehabilitation and adjunct therapies: exercise, physical, speech and occupational therapy, dance, music, acupuncture, cannabis and supplements · also: https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11232530/
- [statement] Two meta-analyses of randomized trials report greater vocal intensity (sound pressure level) after LSVT than with control interventions: one pooled 141 participants and found a higher level with LSVT of 7.36 dB (95% CI 6.60-8.12) immediately after treatment, and the other reported increases of 8.87, 4.34, 3.25 and 3.31 dB for sustained 'Ah' phonation, Rainbow passage reading, monologue and picture description after one month versus no intervention; both sets of authors state that larger randomized trials are needed. (medium confidence) — https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8782619/ · keywords: Parkinson's disease rehabilitation and adjunct therapies: exercise, physical, speech and occupational therapy, dance, music, acupuncture, cannabis and supplements · also: https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/32539227/
- [statement] Two Cochrane reviews with literature searches up to April 2011 each concluded that evidence was insufficient: the review of speech and language therapy versus placebo or no intervention (three randomised trials, 63 participants) found insufficient evidence to conclusively support or refute efficacy for speech problems in Parkinson's disease, and the review comparing therapy techniques (six trials, 159 patients) found insufficient evidence to support or refute any form of therapy over another; the PD COMM authors summarise the earlier review as showing insufficient evidence because of few trials, limited sample sizes and high risk of bias. (medium confidence) — https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7098084/ · keywords: Parkinson's disease rehabilitation and adjunct therapies: exercise, physical, speech and occupational therapy, dance, music, acupuncture, cannabis and supplements · also: https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7120320/, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11232530/
- [statement] In the Berlin LSVT BIG study (60 patients with mild to moderate Parkinson's disease randomly assigned to one-to-one LSVT BIG, group Nordic Walking or unsupervised domestic exercises; UPDRS scores from blinded video rating), the mean UPDRS motor improvement at 16 weeks was -5.05 (SD 3.91) with LSVT BIG versus a mild deterioration of 0.58 (SD 3.17) with Nordic Walking and 1.68 (SD 5.95) with domestic exercise, with no significant group differences in quality of life (PDQ39).
