(medium confidence) — https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/20669294/ · keywords: Parkinson's disease rehabilitation and adjunct therapies: exercise, physical, speech and occupational therapy, dance, music, acupuncture, cannabis and supplements · also: https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3316992/
- [statement] Two small randomised trials of reduced-dose LSVT BIG protocols differ in what they report: a trial of a 2-week short protocol with identical exercises found motor performance equally improved versus standard LSVT BIG, whereas a trial of a modified protocol (twice weekly in clinic and twice weekly at home) reported the standard protocol favoured on some balance and gait measures. (medium confidence) — https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/24872078/ · keywords: Parkinson's disease rehabilitation and adjunct therapies: exercise, physical, speech and occupational therapy, dance, music, acupuncture, cannabis and supplements · also: https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10918598/
- [statement] In the ParkinSong controlled trial of 75 people living with Parkinson's disease, which compared a singing-based intervention with an active control condition at 2 dosage levels (weekly vs monthly) over 3 months, intervention participants showed significant improvements in vocal intensity, maximum expiratory pressure and voice-related quality of life compared with controls, with no statistical differences between groups on maximum phonation length or maximum inspiratory pressure at 3 months; a systematic review describes this trial as a non-randomised controlled trial. (medium confidence) — https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/31081485/ · keywords: Parkinson's disease rehabilitation and adjunct therapies: exercise, physical, speech and occupational therapy, dance, music, acupuncture, cannabis and supplements · also: https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7547481/
- [statement] Two randomised trials of occupational therapy-related interventions in Parkinson's disease reported different primary-outcome results at 3 months: the OTiP trial (home-based occupational therapy versus usual care) reported a result in favour of the intervention on the Canadian Occupational Performance Measure, whereas the PD REHAB trial (physiotherapy and occupational therapy versus no therapy) reported no difference between groups on the Nottingham Extended Activities of Daily Living scale; the two trials differ in intervention, comparator and primary outcome measure. (medium confidence) — https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/24726066/ · keywords: Parkinson's disease rehabilitation and adjunct therapies: exercise, physical, speech and occupational therapy, dance, music, acupuncture, cannabis and supplements · also: https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/25854809/, https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/26785394/
- [statement] Sources differ on whether external cueing reduces freezing of gait (FOG) in Parkinson's disease: the APTA guideline states that physical therapists should implement external cueing to reduce FOG (evidence quality: high; recommendation strength: strong) and a 2020 systematic review concluded that visual and auditory cueing are effective interventions for FOG (evidence level A-), whereas a 2026 meta-analysis of repeated external cueing found no statistically significant reduction in FOG severity versus control and rated the certainty of evidence for all outcomes as low. (medium confidence) — https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9046970/ · keywords: Parkinson's disease rehabilitation and adjunct therapies: exercise, physical, speech and occupational therapy, dance, music, acupuncture, cannabis and supplements · also: https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/31994842/, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC13212247/, https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/37086934/, https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/28890341/
- [statement] In the SURE-PD3 randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled phase 3 trial (298 participants with early PD at 58 US sites; inosine titrated to raise serum urate to 7.1-8.0 mg/dL, n = 149, versus placebo, n = 149, for up to 2 years), the study closed early after a prespecified interim futility analysis and MDS-UPDRS progression rates did not differ significantly (11.1 points per year for inosine versus 9.9 for placebo; difference 1.26, 95% CI -0.59 to 3.11; P = .18); more kidney stones occurred with inosine (7.0 versus 1.4 stones per 100 patient-years) and the authors concluded the findings do not support inosine as a treatment for early PD. (high confidence) — https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8441591/ · keywords: Parkinson's disease rehabilitation and adjunct therapies: exercise, physical, speech and occupational therapy, dance, music, acupuncture, cannabis and supplements · also: https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC13442935/
- [statement] In a double-blind, randomized, controlled, crossover study (Neurology 2017) of single-dose intake in eighteen patients with advanced Parkinson disease, Mucuna pruriens (MP) powder from roasted seeds at a high dose containing 17.5 mg/kg of levodopa induced greater motor improvement at 90 and 180 minutes, longer ON duration and fewer dyskinesias than dispersible levodopa plus benserazide (3.5 mg/kg), and the authors concluded that single-dose MP met all noninferiority efficacy and safety outcome measures; a 2025 systematic review likewise states that this trial found MP significantly reduced dyskinesia at both 90 and 180 min compared to levodopa plus a decarboxylase inhibitor. (high confidence) — https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC5539737/ · keywords: Parkinson's disease rehabilitation and adjunct therapies: exercise, physical, speech and occupational therapy, dance, music, acupuncture, cannabis and supplements · also: https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12377966/
- [statement] Sources differ on adverse events with Mucuna pruriens (MP) in Parkinson disease: a 2025 systematic review (5 clinical trials, 108 participants; one study rated high quality, one with some concerns and three low quality) found MP associated with fewer adverse events and no dyskinesia reported while calling current clinical evidence limited, whereas a 12-month open-label phase 2 randomized trial in thirty-two untreated patients reported more frequent adverse events with MP than with levodopa plus a decarboxylase inhibitor (56% vs. 37.5%, p = 0.48; not statistically significant) and stated that larger double-blind trials with extended follow-up of 24–36 months are needed. (high confidence) (verified as of 2026-11-27) — https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12377966/ · keywords: Parkinson's disease rehabilitation and adjunct therapies: exercise, physical, speech and occupational therapy, dance, music, acupuncture, cannabis and supplements · also: https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC13347555/

## Facts and statements

- [statement] Sham-controlled RCTs of acupuncture for PD-related fatigue found no significant difference between real and sham acupuncture: Kluger et al. (ninety-four PD patients, 6 weeks of biweekly treatment) reported significant improvements in both groups at 6 and 12 weeks without significant between-group differences, and Kong et al. (forty PD patients, 5 weeks) reported the same pattern; the Cui et al. review found fatigue showed no difference from sham (SMD 0.10) and graded certainty for fatigue very low. (high confidence) — https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/27028133/ · keywords: Parkinson's disease rehabilitation and adjunct therapies: exercise, physical, speech and occupational therapy, dance, music, acupuncture, cannabis and supplements · also: https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC5853635/, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC13189933/
- [statement] Authors differ on what sham-controlled acupuncture results imply: Kluger et al. conclude that PD-related fatigue joins the conditions that acupuncture helps primarily through nonspecific or placebo effects, and Kong et al. judge real and sham acupuncture equally effective for PD-related fatigue and likely due to nonspecific or placebo effects, whereas Kwon et al. report that sham acupuncture combined with conventional medicine was superior to conventional medicine alone in their network meta-analysis and suggest that a sham acupuncture-controlled design might underestimate the effect of acupuncture treatment. (medium confidence) — https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/27028133/ · keywords: Parkinson's disease rehabilitation and adjunct therapies: exercise, physical, speech and occupational therapy, dance, music, acupuncture, cannabis and supplements · also: https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC5853635/, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8619200/
- [statement] No serious adverse events were reported in the acupuncture trials and reviews read, although mild-event reporting was inconsistent: an earlier meta-analysis, Kluger et al. and Cui et al. each report no serious adverse events; Yan et al. report no severe adverse events in either group, with the most common self-reported acupuncture-related events being severe tremor; bleeding, numbness, or infection; and sharp pain during treatment; Cui et al. note that reporting of mild adverse events was variable and often not described in detail; and Parkinson's UK lists slight pain, bleeding or bruising, and feeling sick, drowsy or faint as minor, short-lived side effects. (high confidence) (verified as of 2026-11-27) — https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/28917379/ · keywords: Parkinson's disease rehabilitation and adjunct therapies: exercise, physical, speech and occupational therapy, dance, music, acupuncture, cannabis and supplements · also: https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/27028133/, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC13189933/, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11208974/, https://www.parkinsons.org.uk/information/treatments/complementary-therapies
- [statement] Appraisals of the acupuncture-for-PD literature rate its quality low: an overview of 11 systematic reviews and meta-analyses (Huang et al.) rated all included reviews very-low-quality on AMSTAR-2, with GRADE revealing 20 studies with very-low-quality evidence, 9 with low-quality evidence, 3 with moderate-quality evidence, and 0 with high-quality evidence, and its authors say their conclusion must be interpreted cautiously; the York CRD abstract of the Lee et al. review reports that seven RCTs were of low quality, and Noh et al. rated the methodological quality of their included RCTs low. (high confidence) — https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7482669/ · keywords: Parkinson's disease rehabilitation and adjunct therapies: exercise, physical, speech and occupational therapy, dance, music, acupuncture, cannabis and supplements · also: https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK76307/, https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/28917379/
- [statement] The complementary-medicine clinical practice guideline for idiopathic PD (Cho et al.) grades concomitant use of acupuncture and anti-parkinsonian drug therapy as 'should be considered' (strength of recommendation B, level of evidence low; twenty-one RCTs) and moxibustion as 'may be considered' (strength C, level of evidence low). (low confidence) (verified as of 2026-11-27) — https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6196228/ · keywords: Parkinson's disease rehabilitation and adjunct therapies: exercise, physical, speech and occupational therapy, dance, music, acupuncture, cannabis and supplements
- [statement] Systematic reviews and meta-analyses of cannabis or cannabinoids in PD, published between 2022 and 2026, conclude that the evidence does not establish clinical benefit: Urbi et al. report that no compelling evidence was found to recommend the use of cannabis in PD patients, while also identifying a potential benefit with respect to alleviation of PD related tremor, anxiety, pain, improvement of sleep quality and quality of life; Messak et al. report that cannabinoids have not shown significant benefit in PD; Fernandes et al. report that current randomized evidence is insufficient to establish clinically meaningful benefits. (high confidence) — https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/34958046/ · keywords: Parkinson's disease rehabilitation and adjunct therapies: exercise, physical, speech and occupational therapy, dance, music, acupuncture, cannabis and supplements · also: https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/42138778/, https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/42966680/
- [statement] In the Messak et al. meta-analysis of randomized trials of cannabinoids in PD (eleven RCTs identified, six eligible for meta-analysis), cannabinoids did not significantly improve PD severity (SMD = 0.16, p = 0.27), motor examination (SMD=-0.08, p = 0.57) or non-motor symptoms (SMD= -0.03, p = 0.94); the authors state that the nabilone benefit signal for non-motor symptoms represents a distinct question warranting dedicated trials. (low confidence) — https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/42138778/ · keywords: Parkinson's disease rehabilitation and adjunct therapies: exercise, physical, speech and occupational therapy, dance, music, acupuncture, cannabis and supplements
- [statement] Two small randomized crossover trials of cannabinoids for levodopa-induced dyskinesia in PD reported opposite results: Sieradzan et al. (Neurology, 2001; n = 7) reported that nabilone significantly reduced levodopa-induced dyskinesia, whereas Carroll et al. (Neurology, 2004; 19 randomized, seventeen completed) reported no evidence of a treatment effect of oral cannabis extract on levodopa-induced dyskinesia; a systematic review of RCTs in movement disorders states that of three PD RCTs with levodopa-induced dyskinesia as primary outcome, only one, using nabilone, showed a reduction. (medium confidence) — https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/11739835/ · keywords: Parkinson's disease rehabilitation and adjunct therapies: exercise, physical, speech and occupational therapy, dance, music, acupuncture, cannabis and supplements · also: https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/15477546/, https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/35859051/
- [statement] The registry record NCT03582137 (University of Colorado, Denver; cannabidiol for motor symptoms in PD) lists overall status COMPLETED with status verified date 2024-07, lists its phase as PHASE2 with 74 participants enrolled (type ACTUAL), and shows results first posted 2024-07-23. (low confidence) (verified as of 2026-11-27) — https://clinicaltrials.gov/study/NCT03582137 · keywords: Parkinson's disease rehabilitation and adjunct therapies: exercise, physical, speech and occupational therapy, dance, music, acupuncture, cannabis and supplements
- [statement] The registry record NCT06629389 (sponsor Laboratorio Elea Phoenix; a randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial of cannabidiol (Kanbis) in PD listing its phase as PHASE2, with primary outcome adverse events according to CTCAE v5.0) lists overall status RECRUITING with status verified date 2024-09, estimated primary completion 2025-11 and estimated enrollment 88, and shows no posted results. (low confidence) (verified as of 2026-11-27) — https://clinicaltrials.gov/study/NCT06629389 · keywords: Parkinson's disease rehabilitation and adjunct therapies: exercise, physical, speech and occupational therapy, dance, music, acupuncture, cannabis and supplements
- [statement] On dance and motor symptom severity the sources differ: the European Physiotherapy Guideline (first edition, December 2014) gives a weak recommendation against using dance to improve movement functions (UPDRS III), whereas two meta-analyses of randomized trials (Ismail et al., 20 RCTs; Carapellotti et al., sixteen RCTs) report better MDS-UPDRS scores with dance than in non-dancers or no-intervention controls. (medium confidence) (verified as of 2026-11-27) — https://www.parkinsonnet.nl/app/uploads/sites/3/2019/11/eu_guideline_parkinson_guideline_for_pt_s1.pdf · keywords: Parkinson's disease rehabilitation and adjunct therapies: exercise, physical, speech and occupational therapy, dance, music, acupuncture, cannabis and supplements · also: https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8456607/, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7406058/
- [statement] The European Physiotherapy Guideline (first edition, December 2014) gives a strong recommendation for using tai chi to improve movement functions (UPDRS III) and weak recommendations for using it to improve number of falls, balance capacity (BBS), walking speed, stride length, walking distance, functional mobility (TUG), muscle strength and functional reach, based on three CCTs in which 200 pwp participated. (low confidence) (verified as of 2026-11-27) — https://www.parkinsonnet.nl/app/uploads/sites/3/2019/11/eu_guideline_parkinson_guideline_for_pt_s1.pdf · keywords: Parkinson's disease rehabilitation and adjunct therapies: exercise, physical, speech and occupational therapy, dance, music, acupuncture, cannabis and supplements
- [statement] In a systematic review of sixteen RCTs involving 636 participants with mild to moderate PD, Carapellotti et al. reported that dance was favored over no intervention on MDS-UPDRS III (-2.31 points, p = 0.0004; four studies, n = 160) and balance (0.50 points, p = 0.0007; five studies, n = 206) but not on forward gait velocity (p = 0.44) or PDQ-39 (p = 0.65); an umbrella review of 55 systematic reviews (Pinto et al.) reported that dance added to usual care was better than usual care alone for motor symptoms severity, depressive symptoms, balance and functional mobility but not for gait distance and quality of life. (medium confidence) — https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7406058/ · keywords: Parkinson's disease rehabilitation and adjunct therapies: exercise, physical, speech and occupational therapy, dance, music, acupuncture, cannabis and supplements · also: https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11687919/
- [statement] Two randomized trials compared boxing with another active program: in Combs et al. (n = 31; 24-36 sessions of 90 minutes over 12 weeks) the traditional exercise group had significantly greater gains in balance confidence than the boxing group while only the boxing group showed significant improvements in gait velocity and endurance, and in Sangarapillai et al. (40 participants, 20-week trial) the sensory exercise group improved in comparison to the boxing group on a group-by-time interaction for the UPDRS-III (P = .036). (medium confidence) — https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/23422464/ · keywords: Parkinson's disease rehabilitation and adjunct therapies: exercise, physical, speech and occupational therapy, dance, music, acupuncture, cannabis and supplements · also: https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8414806/
- [statement] Adverse-event findings reported in the sources read: the APTA guideline reports that studies found no significant differences in adverse events between community-based exercise and the comparison groups, Li et al. observed no serious adverse events in their tai chi trial, and Ban et al. state that none of the included articles in their yoga meta-analysis reported serious adverse events. (medium confidence) — https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9046970/ · keywords: Parkinson's disease rehabilitation and adjunct therapies: exercise, physical, speech and occupational therapy, dance, music, acupuncture, cannabis and supplements · also: https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3285459/, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8275425/
- [statement] The APTA clinical practice guideline and the Cochrane network meta-analysis state different certainty ratings for aerobic (endurance) exercise and for resistance training: APTA labels both with high evidence quality and strong recommendation strength, while the Cochrane review rates confidence as low for endurance training and for strength/resistance training on the severity of motor signs. (medium confidence) — https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9046970/ · keywords: Parkinson's disease rehabilitation and adjunct therapies: exercise, physical, speech and occupational therapy, dance, music, acupuncture, cannabis and supplements · also: https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11001292/
- [statement] Sources differ on whether exercise or physiotherapy improved quality of life: the APTA guideline, the Cochrane network meta-analysis (low confidence for gait/balance/functional training) and a large physiotherapy meta-analysis report quality-of-life improvements for some interventions, whereas the PD REHAB trial, the earlier Cochrane physiotherapy review and a meta-analysis of aerobic exercise report no significant quality-of-life difference. (medium confidence) — https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9046970/ · keywords: Parkinson's disease rehabilitation and adjunct therapies: exercise, physical, speech and occupational therapy, dance, music, acupuncture, cannabis and supplements · also: https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11001292/, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7564288/, https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/26785394/, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7120224/
- [statement] The trial registry record for NCT04284436 lists SPARX3 as active, not recruiting (status verified 2026-04), with enrollment 370 (actual), primary completion estimated 2027-07-31, last update posted 2026-07-10, and no results posted. (low confidence) (verified as of 2026-11-27) — https://clinicaltrials.gov/api/v2/studies/NCT04284436 · keywords: Parkinson's disease rehabilitation and adjunct therapies: exercise, physical, speech and occupational therapy, dance, music, acupuncture, cannabis and supplements
- [statement] Reviews state that follow-up evidence is limited: the Cochrane physiotherapy review found benefit in most outcomes over the short term (less than 3 months), the aerobic exercise meta-analysis reported no valid evidence on follow-up effects, the physiotherapy meta-analysis by Radder and colleagues stated that it was not possible to perform a meta-analysis on long-term effects, and the Cochrane network meta-analysis analysed effects only up to six weeks after the intervention; the APTA guideline states that gains appear to dissipate if exercise is discontinued. (high confidence) — https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7120224/ · keywords: Parkinson's disease rehabilitation and adjunct therapies: exercise, physical, speech and occupational therapy, dance, music, acupuncture, cannabis and supplements · also: https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4077570/, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7564288/, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11001292/, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9046970/
- [statement] A review by LSVT researchers, two of whom disclose ownership interest in LSVT Global, Inc., tabulates LSVT LOUD and LSVT BIG as standardized protocols with a dosage of 4 consecutive days a week for 4 weeks (16 sessions in one month); the PD COMM trial likewise delivered LSVT LOUD as four sessions each week over four weeks. (high confidence) — https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3316992/ · keywords: Parkinson's disease rehabilitation and adjunct therapies: exercise, physical, speech and occupational therapy, dance, music, acupuncture, cannabis and supplements · also: https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6261685/, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11232530/
- [statement] In a published comparison table of the two programmes, LSVT LOUD directs increased movement amplitude predominately to the respiratory/laryngeal systems whereas LSVT BIG directs it across the limb motor system including gait; the Berlin LSVT BIG study report describes LSVT BIG as focusing on intensive exercising of high-amplitude movements. (high confidence) — https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3316992/ · keywords: Parkinson's disease rehabilitation and adjunct therapies: exercise, physical, speech and occupational therapy, dance, music, acupuncture, cannabis and supplements · also: https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/20669294/
- [statement] In PD COMM, where only adverse events specific to speech and language therapy or serious events related to vocal strain or injury were reported, 93 adverse events (predominately vocal strain) were recorded in the LSVT LOUD group and 46 in the NHS speech and language therapy group, none in the no-therapy group, and no serious adverse events; the authors describe the higher rate of vocal strain with LSVT LOUD as mostly a minor, transient issue. (medium confidence) — https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11232530/ · keywords: Parkinson's disease rehabilitation and adjunct therapies: exercise, physical, speech and occupational therapy, dance, music, acupuncture, cannabis and supplements · also: https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11474952/
- [statement] Randomised trials of remote delivery of LSVT LOUD report outcomes comparable to face-to-face delivery: Constantinescu and colleagues confirmed non-inferiority of online delivery for the primary outcome (mean change in sound pressure level on a monologue task); Theodoros and colleagues, in a single-blinded noninferiority trial (31 participants randomly assigned to face-to-face or online treatment, plus 21 non-metropolitan participants treated online), confirmed noninferiority of online treatment; and a 2025 pilot trial of 20 people comparing teletherapy with face-to-face LSVT LOUD concluded that both appear effective and that larger studies are needed. (medium confidence) — https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/21281410/ · keywords: Parkinson's disease rehabilitation and adjunct therapies: exercise, physical, speech and occupational therapy, dance, music, acupuncture, cannabis and supplements · also: https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/27145396/, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12034115/
- [statement] In the 'art therapy' meta-analysis by Liu and colleagues of 26 randomized controlled trials (2,756 individuals), the included interventions were 5 music, 14 dance, 2 yoga, 1 mindfulness, 1 theater, 1 virtual-reality game-based, 1 Tai Chi plus yoga and 1 Qigong plus dance studies, and the authors conclude that dance therapy exhibited the most pronounced effects across motor function outcomes. (low confidence) — https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12444631/ · keywords: Parkinson's disease rehabilitation and adjunct therapies: exercise, physical, speech and occupational therapy, dance, music, acupuncture, cannabis and supplements
- [statement] On technology-delivered cueing, a technological review of wearable cueing systems for freezing of gait states that novel cueing systems have been evaluated predominantly in laboratory settings, a narrative review states that the increasing use of wearable technology is allowing the cue type, cue content and dose to be adapted to individual patients, and the APTA guideline notes that the cost of utilizing technology for the external cueing source should be considered. (medium confidence) — https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6470562/ · keywords: Parkinson's disease rehabilitation and adjunct therapies: exercise, physical, speech and occupational therapy, dance, music, acupuncture, cannabis and supplements · also: https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/28890341/, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9046970/

## Research summary — Acupuncture, massage and traditional adjuncts in PD

Evidence read for acupuncture, massage, the Alexander Technique and other traditional adjuncts in Parkinson's disease (PD). Two older meta-analyses found no significant UPDRS advantage of real over placebo acupuncture; later syntheses of acupuncture combined with conventional treatment report UPDRS gains but describe the evidence as limited, and an overview rated all included reviews very-low-quality. Sham-controlled trials show a sleep signal and no fatigue benefit over sham. No serious adverse events were reported. Massage meta-analyses report motor benefit alongside methodological concerns. NICE NG71 says to consider the Alexander Technique for balance or motor function problems; a complementary-medicine guideline grades acupuncture added to drugs 'should be considered' on low-level evidence; Parkinson's UK does not endorse any particular therapies.

## Source disagreement — Acupuncture, massage and traditional adjuncts in PD

Kluger et al. and Kong et al. attribute the improvement seen in both arms of sham-controlled fatigue trials to nonspecific or placebo effects, while Kwon et al. suggest a sham acupuncture-controlled design might underestimate the effect of acupuncture treatment.

## Source disagreement — Acupuncture, massage and traditional adjuncts in PD

For electroacupuncture, the Cho et al. guideline reports no significant difference in overall clinical effectiveness in three RCTs, whereas Yu et al. report that electroacupuncture showed the highest overall efficacy among all modalities.

## Research summary — Cannabis and cannabinoids in PD

Systematic reviews and meta-analyses of cannabis and cannabinoids in Parkinson's disease (PD), published 2022 to 2026, report that the evidence does not establish clinical benefit. Individual randomized trials of CBD/THC oils, CBD and nabilone are small and heterogeneous: the Colorado CBD/THC trial and the 2026 São Paulo cannabis-oil trial found no significant difference on their primary outcomes, while one nabilone trial reported a non-motor symptom difference. Reported adverse events include dizziness, confusion and irritability. Positive effects described in uncontrolled studies were not confirmed by small RCTs, per one review. The Parkinson's Foundation does not endorse use for PD symptoms or disease progression. One phase II CBD trial was listed as recruiting in the registry.

## Source disagreement — Cannabis and cannabinoids in PD

Levodopa-induced dyskinesia: Sieradzan et al. report that nabilone significantly reduced it in a crossover trial (n = 7), while Carroll et al. report no treatment effect of oral cannabis extract in a crossover trial.

## Research summary — Dance, tai chi, yoga, boxing and community exercise programs

Group-based exercise modes in Parkinson's disease are described by guidelines and reviews with mixed strength. The APTA guideline gives community-based exercise a strong recommendation with high evidence strength, while the European guideline gives only weak recommendations for dance and a strong one for tai chi on UPDRS III. Randomized trials report better limits-of-stability with tai chi than resistance training or stretching and better MDS-UPDRS-3 with 12 months of tango than no intervention. Meta-analyses diverge on quality of life for tai chi and qigong, on yoga robustness, on Nordic walking benefit and on boxing, and review authors describe dance evidence as low certainty or critically low confidence.

## Source disagreement — Dance, tai chi, yoga, boxing and community exercise programs

The APTA guideline cites its reference 174, the Combs et al. randomized trial, among studies indicating superior balance outcomes for boxing over traditional multi-modal exercise, whereas that trial's abstract reports that the traditional exercise group had significantly greater gains in balance confidence than the boxing group.

## Research summary — Exercise and physical therapy in PD

Guidelines read here (NICE NG71, the APTA physical therapist guideline and the German Society for Neurology guideline) include physiotherapy statements. APTA grades aerobic exercise, resistance training and balance training as high evidence quality with strong recommendations, and flexibility exercises as low and weak. A Cochrane network meta-analysis of 154 RCTs reported benefits for most exercise types, little evidence of differences between types, and confidence from moderate to very low. Sources differ on quality-of-life effects and on high versus moderate intensity, and the PD REHAB trial found no difference in its primary outcome for physiotherapy plus occupational therapy. Reviews describe follow-up evidence as short, and sources differ on whether exercise slows progression. SPARX3, a phase 3 high-intensity treadmill trial, was listed as active, not recruiting, with no results posted.

## Research summary — LSVT BIG, LSVT LOUD and speech-language therapy

LSVT LOUD and LSVT BIG are standardized, intensive programmes (16 sessions over four weeks) that train the amplitude of voice or limb movement. In the PD COMM trial of 388 people, LSVT LOUD lowered self-reported voice handicap versus no therapy and versus NHS speech and language therapy, with benefit still present at 12 months and mostly minor vocal-strain adverse events. Two Cochrane reviews (searches to April 2011) found insufficient evidence; later meta-analyses report higher vocal loudness, while intelligibility results are mixed. NICE NG71 recommends speech and language therapy including attention to effort therapies; RCSLT guidance (December 2025) highly recommends LSVT LOUD. For LSVT BIG, the Berlin trial reported UPDRS motor gains, but a meta-analysis found only trends for walking and rated evidence preliminary.

Gate verdict: `SUPPORTED`. Auxiliary assertion: `prose:3af6c3397e6d2399e2225e643cfa465859562d1a7642e966b29b9d80dcbcf919`. Statement hash: `3af6c3397e6d2399e2225e643cfa465859562d1a7642e966b29b9d80dcbcf919`.

## Source disagreement — LSVT BIG, LSVT LOUD and speech-language therapy

Session length for LSVT LOUD differs by source: Ramig and colleagues describe 16 individual 1-hour sessions in 1 month, whereas PD COMM and the Dutch guideline describe 50-minute sessions four times a week for four weeks.

## Source disagreement — LSVT BIG, LSVT LOUD and speech-language therapy

The Constantinescu abstract reports non-significant main effects for the LSVT environment, dysarthria severity and interaction effects for all outcome measures, whereas the Cochrane review states that sustained phonation loudness did not support the equivalence of online and face-to-face delivery and was significant in favour of face-to-face delivery.

Gate verdict: `SUPPORTED`. Auxiliary assertion: `prose:5fbc9a0f6fe06fe5a11af0a84caa02569b5f510d0d2e93343e89c7f88399980a`. Statement hash: `5fbc9a0f6fe06fe5a11af0a84caa02569b5f510d0d2e93343e89c7f88399980a`.

Sources: [source 1](<https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7120320/>) · [source 2](<https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/21281410/>)

## Source disagreement — LSVT BIG, LSVT LOUD and speech-language therapy

NICE NG71 recommendation 1.7.8 gives attention to effort therapies as its example of speech and communication strategies, whereas RCSLT guidance (December 2025) states that LSVT LOUD is the only behavioural treatment with strong evidence for managing dysarthria.

## Research summary — Music, art and creative therapies in PD

Educational summary of what published sources say, not medical advice. Meta-analyses of rhythmic auditory stimulation and music-based interventions in Parkinson's disease report positive pooled effects on gait velocity and stride length but not cadence, and disagree on balance, timed up-and-go, UPDRS motor scores and freezing of gait. One singing review rates the certainty of its RCT-based finding as very low and another calls singing a promising adjunct therapy, and a trial's own authors limit attribution to singing. Reviews conflict on quality of life, mood and cognition. The visual art therapy evidence cited here is an exploratory observational study, and a meta-analysis calls visual arts and painting a research gap; one art-therapy meta-analysis of 26 trials included 14 dance trials. Review authors repeatedly flag small samples and limited blinding.

## Open question — Music, art and creative therapies in PD

Whether the music-therapy meta-analysis of thirty-three studies including 3635 patients is supported on full-text review is not established here, because only its PubMed abstract is in the pinned body.

## Research summary — Occupational therapy, cueing and gait training

What published sources report about occupational therapy, external cueing and gait training in Parkinson's disease. NICE guideline NG71 and an AOTA practice guideline address occupational therapy. The OTiP trial reported a favourable primary outcome, the PD REHAB trial reported no difference on its primary outcome, and a Cochrane review found insufficient evidence. The APTA guideline rates external cueing and gait training as high evidence quality with strong recommendation strength, yet meta-analyses differ on the best cue modality, and a 2026 meta-analysis found no significant reduction in freezing-of-gait severity. Treadmill meta-analyses report improved walking speed but not cadence. Authors describe cueing durability as unclear and wearable cueing as evaluated mainly in laboratories. This is an attributed summary of sources, not medical advice.

## Source disagreement — Occupational therapy, cueing and gait training

OTiP reported a favourable primary outcome for home-based occupational therapy at 3 months, whereas PD REHAB reported no difference in its primary outcome for physiotherapy plus occupational therapy versus no therapy.

## Source disagreement — Occupational therapy, cueing and gait training

The APTA guideline recommends external cueing to reduce freezing of gait, whereas a 2026 meta-analysis of repeated external cueing found no statistically significant reduction in FOG severity.

## Source disagreement — Occupational therapy, cueing and gait training

Cue modality: a 2013 meta-analysis favoured auditory cueing, a 2026 network meta-analysis reported that somatosensory and visual cues outperformed standalone auditory stimulation, and a 2024 review found that adding visual cueing to walking training did not improve walking speed or stride length.

## Research summary — Supplements: CoQ10, creatine, vitamin D, Mucuna and failed neuroprotectants

Trial evidence for supplements and failed neuroprotectants in Parkinson disease is largely negative in the sources read. Large trials of coenzyme Q10 (QE3), creatine (NET-PD LS-1), inosine (SURE-PD3) and isradipine (STEADY-PD III) each reported no clinical benefit, as did a tocopherol trial. Earlier signals, a CoQ10 dosage-ranging trial reporting a positive trend and a creatine futility screen that did not reject it, were followed by later large trials reporting no benefit. Vitamin D reports are mixed. Mucuna pruriens trials are small and short, and commercial products varied widely from labelled levodopa. NICE NG71 recommends against vitamin E and, except in the context of clinical trials, against co-enzyme Q10 as neuroprotective therapy, recommends that creatine supplements not be offered, and advises a vitamin D supplement. This summarizes what sources report; it is not medical advice.

## Source disagreement — Supplements: CoQ10, creatine, vitamin D, Mucuna and failed neuroprotectants

A 2002 CoQ10 dosage-ranging trial reported a significant 1200-mg/d versus placebo difference (P =.04) and concluded CoQ10 appears to slow functional decline, while the 2014 QE3 phase III trial reported no evidence of clinical benefit.
